A senior UAE official warned that the Gulf must be prepared for a “long period of uncertainty” in which the US and Iran are not able to come to a political settlement to end their war, leaving the region in a state of limbo.
"We should... prepare for a long period of uncertainty in which neither a decisive resolution nor stable regional order can be taken for granted,” Anwar Gargash, the diplomatic advisor to UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed, said on Monday at a forum in Abu Dhabi.
Gargash’s remarks come as the Middle East tries to decipher whether US President Donald Trump will launch fresh strikes on Iran.
Expectations of a new attack were high until last week, when on 3 November the Democrats won a sweeping midterm election victory that Trump and Vice President JD Vance attributed to the unpopularity of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Trump told CNN on Monday it was “highly unlikely” he would attack while negotiations are ongoing.

One of the world’s leading scholars of Ottoman history, Engin Deniz Akarli, died in his home in Istanbul on Sunday, aged 81.
Professor Akarli’s research focused on the legal, political and economic history of the late Ottoman Empire, as well as the Middle East. His scholarship engaged deeply with neglected areas of research in these fields.
One of his most influential works, The Long Peace: Ottoman Lebanon, 1861-1920 (University of California Press, 1993) challenged Eurocentric narratives on state-building and governance that centre western intervention through a close study of the Mount Lebanon Mutassarifiya (governorate) following the civil war of 1860.
He demonstrated that Lebanese self-rule, institutions and local religious reconciliation in this period laid the foundations for secular democracy that was hampered by European intervention.
Born in the northwestern Turkish city of Eskisehir, Professor Akarli completed his primary and secondary education at Eskisehir Maarif College, and graduated from the Department of Business Administration and Economics at the prestigious Robert College (now Bogazici University), in 1968.
He continued his education in the United States, first at Wisconsin University for his Master’s studies, and then at Princeton for his PhD.
His teaching career spanned several universities multiple continents. After completing his doctoral studies, he returned to Turkey as one of the founding professors of the history department at Bogazici University.

A sand embankment collapsed on tents sheltering displaced Palestinians in the Gaza Strip late on Sunday, killing three children and two women as severe weather battered the territory.
At least five other people were rescued with injuries by Civil Defence search-and-rescue teams at the makeshift camp in Deir al-Balah, where operations to locate missing people continued.
Mahmoud Basal, spokesperson for the Palestinian Civil Defence in Gaza, said the massive sandy embankment and surrounding mounds of earth collapsed after a low-pressure weather system brought torrential rain and strong winds to the Strip over the weekend.
Two of those killed were identified as Mariam Nabhan and her son, Salah Nabhan. The other three were Reem al-Zain, Habiba al-Zain and Ibrahim al-Zain.
Weekend downpours flooded an estimated 70,000 temporary tents sheltering displaced families across Gaza, leaving thousands of people exposed to the elements.
Palestinians have blamed Israel’s genocide and ongoing siege for the worsening conditions facing displaced people.
“This is not simply the result of severe weather. It is the direct consequence of prolonged Israeli genocide, the widespread destruction of infrastructure, continued displacement, and the denial of essential humanitarian assistance and adequate shelter,” the Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Saturday.
The ministry said nearly two million Palestinians were living in approximately 270,000 tents across Gaza in “appalling humanitarian conditions”.

Saudi Aramco building in Riyadh damaged by falling debris in attempted attack, ministry says
An administrative building belonging to state oil giant Saudi Aramco in Riyadh was damaged by falling debris following an attempted attack on Sunday, with no injuries or fatalities reported, the kingdom's Energy Ministry said.
A witness told Reuters that they saw blown-out windows across several floors of the Aramco Tower, one of the tallest buildings in the capital's King Abdullah Financial District.
The incident, which the ministry said caused limited damage, came after the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted two missiles fired by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis towards Riyadh.
Aramco was not immediately available for comment, and there was no immediate statement from the Houthis.
Multiple loud booms were heard in Riyadh earlier on Sunday, a Reuters witness said, shortly after Saudi Civil Defense issued an early-warning alert of a potential threat in the region. Authorities later announced that the danger had passed.
The Saudi-led coalition subsequently said it had intercepted and destroyed two cruise missiles in Riyadh and the kingdom's southern region.
Reporting by Reuters

Iran’s ambassador to Moscow Kazem Jalali has said Iran and Russia have discussed strengthening military and security cooperation, with Tehran stressing that talks with the US could not end the conflict without credible guarantees, according to Mehr News Agency.
Jalali said that during a three-hour meeting, Major General Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, briefed Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tehran’s strategic priorities, including accelerating construction of the Rasht-Astara railway and completing the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC).
Jalali said Rezaei conveyed Tehran’s position that negotiations with Washington could not end the conflict without credible guarantees, citing repeated "US violations of commitments" during previous diplomatic engagements, Mehr reported.
He said Rezaei also explained Iran’s response to a letter from US Vice President JD Vance, stressing that dialogue alone could not provide a basis for ending the war.
According to Jalali, Rezaei cited several instances in which Iran had come under attack during diplomatic initiatives, including negotiations in Oman and Geneva, as well as engagements surrounding the Islamabad MoU.
The ambassador said Tehran had made acceptance of its seven strategic conditions by Washington a prerequisite for any new diplomatic initiative. He added that Moscow understood Iran’s position and agreed that commitments had to be implemented.

Paraguay's pro-Israel former president taken into custody over banking crisis
Paraguayan prosecutors charged pro-Israel ex-president Santiago Pena and took him into custody Saturday over a banking crisis that saw millions cut off from their money and sparked major protests.
Pena, Paraguay's youngest-ever president, was removed from office by the Senate on Friday, just three days after the collapse of a leading bank with which he had business links.
An indictment against Pena states that "between 2023 and 2026, UENO BANK S.A. allegedly received deposits and loans from public and pension entities" and that it "was also allegedly granting loans to companies linked to the bank's economic group in an irregular manner."
The 47-year-old economist owned shares in Ueno Holding, the controlling company of the bank, until he sold them last year.

Israeli restrictions have meant scarce aid- and in particular, shelter materials- is entering the strip, leaving almost all of Gaza's population exposed to the elements and health risks amid rapidly deteriorating sanitation conditions.
Abu Ramdan emphasised that the razing of infrastructure by Israel as part of its onslaught on Gaza has amplified the health risks. Abu Ramadan also emphasised that widespread malnutrition, particularly among children and pregnant women, means their bodies will be less able to fight off infections.
"What is happening in Gaza is not a passing winter crisis, but an escalating threat to public health and people's lives that requires immediate international action commensurate with the scale of the catastrophe," Abu Ramadan said.

There is nothing particularly unusual about an election stunt. Politicians routinely perform them. Rarely, though, is a stunt as obvious as the one US President Donald Trump pulled on 3 November, Election Day, when he announced that America would, at year's end, stop providing $4bn in annual military aid to Israel.
Trump had clearly read the room, and the polls.
For all his public disdain for polls he claims are "fake" or "rigged", the president understands their political significance.
Polling data suggests that American voters are increasingly uncomfortable contributing their tax dollars to Israel's military, particularly as costs rise in the US and Americans struggle to afford basic necessities.
An August Marquette Law School poll, for example, found that 52 percent of American adults believe Washington provides Israel with too much military aid. Only 16 percent said it provides too little. Even among Republicans under 30, 54 percent said Washington gives Israel too much.
Appearing on Fox & Friends that morning, Trump asked why Republicans should "suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed", a reference to Abdul El-Sayed, who hours later would become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. US President Donald Trump said on Friday that the American military carried out a new round of "minor strikes" on Iran's Qeshm Island, which he claimed "knocked out" Iranian air defence systems.
Iranian state media reported that two blasts were heard in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, which lies in the Strait of Hormuz, the contested waterway which has been disrupted since the US launched its assault on Iran in February.
The Iranian army said in comments carried by state broadcaster IRIB that their air defences downed a US drone over the island.
But Trump told reporters shortly after that the attacks "knocked out" the air defence systems "in about 15 minutes, maybe five".
Responding to reports of the explosions, US Central Command (Centcom) said that the situation is "relatively calm".
In a post on X late on Friday, it said that the US is “offering a reward of up to $20 million and possible relocation for information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community, or the movement of any of the above”.
This comes after the US military reported that it had conducted what it described as "defensive strikes" on Monday.
The latest round of strikes is the first since Trump's Republican Party suffered a crushing defeat in the US midterm elections- a loss which was fuelled in part by Trump's war on Iran and subsequent rocketing of energy prices.
Since then, Trump's messaging has been erratic- oscillating between threats to "destroy" Iran and claims that the war is close to being concluded.

US-Israeli former soldier on visit to Netherlands accused of Gaza war crimes
The Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF) has filed a criminal complaint in the Netherlands against a former US-Israeli soldier accused of involvement in attacks on schools sheltering displaced Palestinians, mass detentions and the destruction of residential buildings in Gaza.
The complaint, submitted to the Dutch National Public Prosecutor's Office on 4 November, names Noam Himmelman, a former member of the Israeli army's Netzah Yehuda Battalion, who is currently in Amsterdam.
HRF alleges that Himmelman was involved in war crimes, crimes against humanity and acts of genocide during Israel's war on Gaza. The complaint was filed under the Dutch International Crimes Act, which allows prosecution of international crimes when suspects are present on Dutch territory.
According to HRF, Israeli forces, including the battalion, surrounded schools in Beit Hanoun on 16 April 2024, where thousands of displaced Palestinians had sought shelter. Soldiers allegedly fired on the school complex and detained dozens of men, including elderly people and teenagers, forcing them to strip before taking them away.
HRF says Himmelman documented the arrests in an Instagram story that it subsequently verified and geolocated to a military outpost near the school.
The foundation also alleges that between January and July 2025, the battalion conducted controlled demolitions of residential buildings across Beit Hanoun, contributing to the extensive destruction of the town. Himmelman served with the unit during these operations.
The complaint cites the battalion's previous record of alleged abuses, including the 2022 death of 78-year-old Palestinian-American Omar Assad after he was detained by its soldiers.

'It would facilitate Gaza genocide': Protesters storm Microsoft planned site
Several hundred activists occupied the construction site of a planned Microsoft data centre in Amsterdam on Friday, protesting the technology giant's alleged role in facilitating Israel's genocide in Gaza, as well as the environmental impact of artificial intelligence infrastructure.
The demonstration, organised by climate and justice collective Geef Tegengas and environmental group Fossielvrij, halted construction work for the day in the city's Sloterdijk district.
The protesters argued that the facility could be used to support AI-powered warfare and Israel's military operations in Gaza.
"It's so many things, so many struggles that come together in this data centre," Nathan Timmer, a spokesman for Geef Tegengas, told AFP.
Timmer, 30, accused the project of helping to facilitate "AI warfare" and what he described as the "genocide" in Gaza.
Dutch news agency ANP reported that police arrested between 150 and 200 protesters, while others left voluntarily.
The protest was part of a wider two-day mobilisation across Europe called by the Stop Dirty Data Centers coalition, which is demanding a pause in the construction of new data centre facilities.

Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty says that he has discussed with Saudi Arabia's Foreign Minister, Prince Faisal bin Farhan, the need to sustain joint efforts to "prevent escalation, restore calm, and pursue the path of negotiations".
Abdelatty said that in a phone call for UAE foreign minister on Friday, he discussed efforts to "restore calm, prevent escalation and prioritise diplomacy", while in another call with his Kuwaiti counterpart, he emphasised "the importance of supporting de-escalation, urging all parties to reduce tensions and prioritise negotiation".
In another post on X, Abdelatty said he discussed with European High Representative "our strategic partnership, de-escalation efforts, advancing negotiations and implementing Gaza peace plan".
